clue.text: New, like Bacon's instrument of science found with hesitation after a month

definitions.text: New, like Bacon's instrument of science

indicators.note: the hesitation sound is placed after the month in the finished word

parts.note: Nov is the standard short form of November
um is the sound a speaker makes while hesitating

explanation.surface: A new scientific tool, Bacon's style, turns up after a month of dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Bacon's treatise on scientific method is the Novum Organum, the 'new instrument'; the answer is its Latin word for new.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adjective in the title of Bacon's Novum Organum means new, the quality of his proposed instrument of reasoning.

clue.text: Not exactly a dream description of Peacock's convent

explanation.surface: Something less than a pleasant reverie is how Peacock's religious house is described.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Love Peacock wrote the satirical novel Nightmare Abbey; an abbey is the 'convent'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad dream is hardly a dream in the pleasant sense, and the word names the abbey in Peacock's satirical novel.

clue.text: Bond villain offers a short book on physical education

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: vol. is the short form of volume, a book

explanation.surface: A James Bond baddie produces a brief volume about PE.
explanation.walkthrough: Fiona Volpe is the villainess of Thunderball.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiona Volpe is the assassin who works for SPECTRE in the Bond story Thunderball.

clue.text: Clue not to be forgotten

parts.note: read as a clue whose purpose is that something not be forgotten: a memory aid

explanation.definitionFit: A memory aid is a device, like a rhyme, that prompts recall so a fact stays remembered.

clue.text: Shakespearean suitor morphs into horse

indicators.note: to morph is to change shape, so the letters of the following words change into a new form

explanation.surface: A suitor from Shakespeare turns into a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of INTO HORSE are rearranged. Hortensio is a suitor of Bianca in The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Hortensio woos Bianca in The Taming of the Shrew, making him one of the play's suitors.

clue.text: Lively wave

parts.note: Lively is the novelist Penelope Lively, one of whose novels has a title whose second word is wave; the missing first word is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lively' looks like an adjective, but it is Penelope Lively, whose 1996 novel is Heat Wave.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Lively's novel title pairs this word with wave, naming a spell of very hot weather.

clue.text: Rex in Medea to be studied again

indicators.note: the letters are 'to be' made into something else, a light signal that they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A king appears in Medea, to be looked at once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of REX IN MEDEA are rearranged; the anagram signal is only the faint 'to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be examined a second time is to be looked over or scrutinised again.

clue.text: Isolated nymph

parts.note: a nymph of Greek myth whose name was given to a place set apart by sea

explanation.walkthrough: Euboea was a nymph, daughter of the river god Asopus, and gave her name to the large Greek island; 'isolated' hints at an island.
explanation.definitionFit: The nymph's name belongs also to a Greek island, land isolated by the Aegean sea.

clue.text: Barker's oath

explanation.surface: A pledge sworn by someone named Barker.
explanation.walkthrough: Clive Barker's 1996 novel is Sacrament; the Latin sacramentum was a Roman soldier's oath of allegiance, an old sense the English word keeps.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of a Clive Barker novel, and in an old sense the word means a solemn pledge sworn before witnesses.

clue.text: Scenarist suggests first test in poems

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the word for poems

parts.note: odes are lyric poems

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word test is used

explanation.surface: A screenwriter recommends sitting an initial exam in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Clifford Odets was an American playwright who also wrote film scripts.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford Odets wrote screenplays in Hollywood as well as stage dramas, so he was a scenarist.

clue.text: An excellent period of Darwin and Austin

definitions.text: An excellent period of Darwin and Austin

parts.words: An excellent period of Darwin and Austin
parts.note: a phrase for a time of greatest flourishing, also used as a title by the poets Erasmus Darwin and Alfred Austin

explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Austin, the Victorian poet laureate, wrote a satire with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A time of highest achievement or prosperity is described with this phrase, from the first age of classical myth.

clue.text: Australian novelist does not quite reach the lengths of Godot's creator

indicators.text: does not quite reach the lengths of
indicators.note: the surname stops short, falling two letters shy of its full length

parts.note: Samuel Beckett wrote Waiting for Godot

explanation.surface: An Australian writer falls short of matching Beckett's stature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does not quite reach the lengths of' trims the last two letters, TT, from BECKETT. Louis Becke wrote South Sea stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Becke was an Australian writer of South Sea adventure stories and novels around 1900.

clue.text: Hughes's game in Room at the Top?

definitions.text: Hughes's game in Room at the Top?

parts.words: Hughes's game in Room at the Top?
parts.note: Ted Hughes's poem The Thought-Fox has the animal, a hunted quarry, entering the dark hole of the head, the room at the top

explanation.walkthrough: Room at the Top is a John Braine novel, but here it is the head, where Hughes's fox arrives in The Thought-Fox.
explanation.definitionFit: A fox is the quarry, the game, in Hughes's poem, which ends with it entering the poet's head.

clue.text: French writer from Arab isle

indicators.note: the writer is made from these letters, worked up out of them in a new order

explanation.surface: A French author hails from an Arabian island.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of ARAB ISLE are rearranged; François Rabelais wrote Gargantua and Pantagruel.
explanation.definitionFit: François Rabelais was the sixteenth-century French author of Gargantua and Pantagruel.

clue.text: Heretical stoic cited unexpectedly

indicators.note: the letters fall out in a surprising new order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Stoic philosopher was quoted as a heretic, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of STOIC CITED are rearranged. Docetism held that Christ only seemed to have a body.
explanation.definitionFit: Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was only apparent, was condemned as a heresy by the early Church.

clue.text: Thucydides defended it vigorously

parts.note: the historian was the Athenian general sent to protect a Thracian city in 424 BC, which fell before he arrived

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is ironic: Thucydides failed to save the city from Brasidas and was exiled for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian colony in Thrace was the city Thucydides was sent to relieve and lost, leading to his exile.

clue.text: His work not exactly averse, say

definitions.text: His work not exactly averse, say

parts.words: His work not exactly averse, say
parts.note: 'averse' is heard as 'a verse'; the writer's work is not exactly in verse, yet is poetic

explanation.walkthrough: 'averse', said aloud, is 'a verse': this writer produces poetry in prose.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of poetic prose produces work that is lyrical but not set out in metrical lines.

clue.text: We hear net result from political writer

indicators.note: the word is judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a web is what netting makes, a mesh

explanation.surface: We are told the final outcome comes from a commentator on politics.
explanation.walkthrough: Sidney and Beatrice Webb were Fabian writers on politics and society.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidney and Beatrice Webb wrote on socialism and founded the London School of Economics.

clue.text: Character in one of "the Roman plays", on stage and in the pit

definitions.text: Character in one of "the Roman plays", on stage and in the pit

parts.words: Character in one of "the Roman plays", on stage and in the pit
parts.note: a figure from Titus Andronicus whose murdered body is thrown into a pit during the play

explanation.walkthrough: 'the pit' is not the theatre's stalls but the pit in the forest where the body of Saturninus's brother is hidden in Titus Andronicus.
explanation.definitionFit: Bassianus, brother of the emperor in Titus Andronicus, is murdered and his corpse is thrown into a pit.

clue.text: Shaw wrote of where these relicts lived

definitions.text: Shaw wrote of where these relicts lived

parts.words: Shaw wrote of where these relicts lived
parts.note: Shaw's first play is named after the houses of men whose wives have died, relicts in the old sense of survivors

explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's first play is Widowers' Houses (1892); 'relict' once meant a surviving spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A relict, in the old sense, is a survivor of a marriage partner, a bereaved husband here.

clue.text: They may take trips in autobiographies

definitions.text: They may take trips in autobiographies

parts.words: They may take trips in autobiographies
parts.note: selves go on self-indulgent 'trips', the idiom for vain self-display, as in memoirs

explanation.walkthrough: An 'ego trip' is self-indulgent display; autobiographies are where writers' selves indulge in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Selves, a person's sense of self-importance, are what go on vain trips in memoirs.

clue.text: Mass movement started by Arnold going to America

parts.note: Benedict Arnold, the American general who turned traitor
US is the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A popular movement begun by Arnold spreads to the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass movement' is not a popular uprising but a section of the Mass. Benedict Arnold supplies the first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Benedictus is a section of the sung Mass, one of the movements in a musical setting.

clue.text: Hardy collaborator may be a plant

explanation.surface: Hardy's partner might turn out to be a shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: Stan Laurel partnered Oliver Hardy in film comedy; the surface wants Thomas Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel was Oliver Hardy's comic partner, and the bay tree is an evergreen shrub of the same name.

clue.text: "- -—!'tis the hour of love" Byron, Don Juan

definitions.text: "- -—!'tis the hour of love" Byron, Don Juan

parts.words: "- -—!'tis the hour of love" Byron, Don Juan
parts.note: the missing opening words of a line in Byron's Don Juan, the Latin greeting to the Virgin that names the evening prayer

explanation.walkthrough: Don Juan, canto III, has 'Ave Maria! 'tis the hour of prayer! … 'tis the hour of love!'
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin greeting to the Virgin opens the evening prayer that Byron's stanza celebrates at twilight.

clue.text: A graduate about to produce a paper ingredient

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate
ca. is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A graduate is set to make something that goes into paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Abaca is Manila hemp, a fibre used in making strong paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Manila hemp fibre from the abaca plant is pulped for tea bags and banknote stock.

clue.text: Shiloh priest, a son of Belial

explanation.surface: A priest at Shiloh was a worthless man.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1 Samuel, Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, priests at Shiloh, are called 'sons of Belial', that is, wicked men.
explanation.definitionFit: Hophni served as a priest at the Shiloh shrine and Scripture brands Eli's sons worthless, sons of Belial.

clue.text: Astronomers may well act according to him

definitions.text: Astronomers may well act according to him

parts.words: Astronomers may well act according to him
parts.note: the idiom 'according to' a rule-book author, meaning by the rules, named after a writer on card games who shares his surname with a famous astronomer

explanation.walkthrough: 'According to Hoyle' means by the rules, after Edmond Hoyle's book on card games; Fred Hoyle was an astronomer.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmond Hoyle codified card games, giving the idiom for correct conduct, and Fred Hoyle was a leading Cambridge astronomer.

clue.text: Model takes directions, becoming a murderess

indicators.note: the first piece takes on the second, which follows it

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car, giving T
E and S stand for the compass points east and south, here east, south, south

explanation.surface: A fashion model obeys instructions and turns into a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles stabs Alec d'Urberville and is hanged for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's heroine Tess Durbeyfield kills Alec d'Urberville, so she is a woman who commits murder.

clue.text: Fondness shown by Marguerite Duras for Hersey work?

definitions.text: shown by Marguerite Duras for Hersey work?

explanation.surface: Marguerite Duras shows her affection for a book by John Hersey.
explanation.walkthrough: John Hersey wrote Hiroshima; Duras wrote the screenplay Hiroshima mon amour, so this is what she showed for 'Hiroshima'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word means love or affection, and Duras's screenplay title declares it for Hiroshima, Hersey's subject.

clue.text: His achievement is history

parts.note: 'is history' sounds like 'is over and done', but this man's achievement was writing historical works

explanation.walkthrough: G. M. Trevelyan was the Cambridge historian of England; 'is history' normally means 'is finished'.
explanation.definitionFit: G. M. Trevelyan wrote English Social History, so his life's work consists of historical writing.

clue.text: Prince of Thieves in crater

explanation.surface: Robin Hood lurks inside a hole in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Autolycus is the master thief of Greek myth and the rogue of The Winter's Tale; a lunar crater bears his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Autolycus, grandfather of Odysseus, was the greatest thief of myth, and a Moon crater is named after him.

clue.text: Eliot's Tireseas, and similar forward looking characters ()

definitions.text: Eliot's Tireseas, and similar forward looking characters

parts.words: Eliot's Tireseas, and similar forward looking characters
parts.note: Tiresias, the blind prophet of The Waste Land, and other figures who see into the future

explanation.walkthrough: Tiresias, the blind prophet, narrates part of Eliot's The Waste Land.
explanation.definitionFit: Prophets like Tiresias foresee the future, which is what forward-looking characters do.
